title: Estimating the reproducibility of psychological science
authors: Open Science Collaboration
key_findings: 100 studies from three 2008 psychology journals were replicated with high-powered designs.
35 of 97 replications (36%) were significant in the original direction vs 97% of originals; mean effect size fell from .403 to .197.
By journal/area: JPSP social 23%, JEP:LMC cognitive 48%, Psych Science social 29%, Psych Science cognitive 53% significant replications.
Replication success tracked the strength of the original evidence.
practical_applications: Treat single famous social-psychology findings as provisional; prefer meta-analyses and large replications when writing 'science says' content.
Cognitive effects replicated more often than social ones in this sample.
limitations: One replication per study; sample of three journals only.
Gilbert et al. (2016) technical comment disputed the interpretation; OSC replied.
license: copyrighted (author version posted with AAAS permission)

title: Many Labs 2: Investigating variation in replicability across samples and settings
authors: Klein, R. A., et al.
key_findings: Preregistered replications of 28 findings; each protocol run in ~half of 125 samples, 15,305 participants, 36 countries/territories.
15 of 28 (54%) significant in the original direction at p < .05 (14, 50%, at p < .0001); 21 (75%) had smaller effects than the original; 9 (32%) went in the opposite direction.
Median Cohen's d: 0.60 original vs 0.15 replication; 16 (57%) replications had d < .20.
Little heterogeneity from task order, lab vs online, or WEIRD vs less-WEIRD samples: variation was more attributable to the effect than to sample/setting.
practical_applications: An effect that fails does not usually 'work only in some cultures'; an effect that works tends to work broadly. Relevant when importing Western findings to Thai audiences.
limitations: Only 28 effects; mostly short online/lab tasks.
Read from the LSE author manuscript (accepted version).

title: A multilab preregistered replication of the ego-depletion effect
authors: Hagger, M. S., Chatzisarantis, N. L. D., et al.
key_findings: Registered Replication Report: 23 labs, total N = 2,141, standardized sequential-task protocol based on Sripada et al.
Ego-depletion effect d = 0.04, 95% CI [-0.07, 0.15] - small, CI includes zero.
Motivated by an earlier meta-analysis reporting a medium-sized effect and later meta-analyses that questioned its size and flagged possible bias.
practical_applications: Do not write stories or captions claiming 'willpower is a battery that runs out' as fact.
limitations: Critics (e.g. Dang 2016 commentary) argue the e-crossing manipulation may not have been depleting; a null for one paradigm is not proof the theory is wrong in every form.
Read from the KOPS (Konstanz) repository copy.

title: Behavioral priming: it's all in the mind, but whose mind?
authors: Doyen, S., Klein, O., Pichon, C.-L., Cleeremans, A.
key_findings: Experiment 1: replication of Bargh, Chen & Burrows (1996) with automated (infrared) timing and a larger sample found no walking-speed priming effect.
Experiment 2: a walking-speed effect appeared only when experimenters were led to expect slower walking - experimenter expectations helped produce the effect.
Debriefing suggested participants were aware of the primes; authors conclude behavioural priming, while real, involves different mechanisms than usually assumed.
practical_applications: Avoid 'show old-age words and people slow down' type claims; subtle-word social priming is weak evidence.
limitations: Bargh disputed the study publicly; the paper itself was not read in full this session.

title: Reconstruction of a train wreck: How priming research went off the rails
authors: Schimmack, U., Heene, M., Kesavan, K.
key_findings: R-Index analysis of the 12 articles cited in the priming chapter (ch. 4) of Thinking, Fast and Slow: 11 of 12 had R-Index below 50.
Kahneman responded that behavioural priming effects 'cannot be as large and as robust as my chapter suggested' (as quoted in secondary coverage).
practical_applications: Use Thinking, Fast and Slow for the System 1/2 framing and heuristics, but not its social-priming chapter.
limitations: Blog post by the critics themselves, not peer reviewed.

title: Thinking, Fast and Slow
authors: Kahneman, D.
key_findings: Existence and edition confirmed (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 2011). Content not read this session.
practical_applications: Background framing for fast intuitive vs slow deliberate thinking; check each specific claim against replication literature (see Schimmack2017).
limitations: Popular book; priming chapter is not well supported by later replications.

title: Assessing the robustness of power posing: No effect on hormones and risk tolerance in a large sample of men and women
authors: Ranehill, E., Dreber, A., Johannesson, M., Leiberg, S., Sul, S., Weber, R. A.
key_findings: N = 200 (original N = 42), experimenter blind to condition, >95% power.
Power posing raised self-reported feelings of power but had no significant effect on hormones or any of three behavioural tasks.
practical_applications: A posture can change how people say they feel, but don't claim it changes hormones or performance.
limitations: Conceptual (not exact) replication.

title: Power posing: P-curving the evidence
authors: Simmons, J. P., Simonsohn, U.
key_findings: P-curve of the 33 studies cited by Carney, Cuddy & Yap (2015) did not show evidential value (flat p-curve) once selective reporting is considered.
Original first author Dana Carney later stated she no longer believes power-pose effects are real (separate statement).
practical_applications: Classic example of a viral pop-psych claim to avoid in content.
limitations: Cuddy, Schultz & Fosse (2018) ran their own p-curve on a broader set and claimed evidential value for felt power; critics say it mixed effect directions. Not read directly.

title: Replicating patterns of prospect theory for decision under risk
authors: Ruggeri, K., et al.
key_findings: Replication of the Kahneman & Tversky (1979) choice items with N = 4,098 (author manuscript) from 19 countries, 13 languages.
Results replicated for 94% of the 17 choice items and 12 of 13 theoretical contrasts; effects were at most attenuated vs 1979.
About a third of participants knew of loss aversion; awareness had only a very modest effect on choices.
practical_applications: Loss framing ('what you lose by squinting every day') is on firmer ground than social priming.
limitations: Hypothetical choices; Thailand not necessarily among the 19 countries (not checked).
Read the Oxford ORA author manuscript ('Not lost in translation'); it tests prospect-theory choice patterns, not the size of loss aversion directly.
Spot-check U3 2026-11-25 applied.

title: Bad is stronger than good
authors: Baumeister, R. F., Bratslavsky, E., Finkenauer, C., Vohs, K. D.
key_findings: Across everyday events, trauma, relationships, social networks, interactions, feedback and learning, bad events have more impact than good ones.
Bad impressions and stereotypes form faster and resist disconfirmation more than good ones; 'hardly any exceptions' found.
Cites Gottman (1994): stable relationships need at least ~5 positive interactions per negative one.
practical_applications: One bad shop experience outweighs several good ones - service stories should show repair, not only delight.
In Mint & Tao conflicts, one harsh line needs several warm beats to recover.
limitations: Narrative review, not meta-analysis; the 5:1 ratio is Gottman's index cited by the review, not a universal law.

title: Duration neglect in retrospective evaluations of affective episodes
authors: Fredrickson, B. L., Kahneman, D.
key_findings: Study 1 (32 Ss) and Study 2 (96 Ss) with film clips: duration had small effects on retrospective evaluations.
Evaluations behave like a weighted average of 'snapshots'; a peak & end rule accounted for 94% of variance in an earlier procedure dataset, duration only 3% more.
practical_applications: Endings and the strongest moment dominate memory of a clip or a shop visit: design a clear peak and a warm last beat.
limitations: Authors themselves urge caution about partial correlations; later work (secondary) suggests day-long experiences may not follow peak-end.

title: The psychology of curiosity: A review and reinterpretation
authors: Loewenstein, G.
key_findings: Curiosity is a cognitively induced deprivation arising from a perceived gap in knowledge (information-gap theory).
Earlier theories missed why people voluntarily seek curiosity and its intensity, transience, link to impulsivity and tendency to disappoint once satisfied.
practical_applications: Open a specific, answerable gap on slide 1 and close it on the last slide.
limitations: Abstract content known only through secondary pages this session.

title: The wick in the candle of learning: Epistemic curiosity activates reward circuitry and enhances memory
authors: Kang, M. J., Hsu, M., Krajbich, I. M., Loewenstein, G., McClure, S. M., Wang, J. T., Camerer, C. F.
key_findings: Curiosity about trivia questions was an inverted-U function of confidence, peaking near 50% confidence (r = .44 with P(1-P)).
Curiosity correlated with caudate activity (reward anticipation); people paid tokens/waiting time to learn answers.
Higher curiosity predicted better recall of surprising answers 1-2 weeks later.
practical_applications: Best hooks are questions the viewer half-knows ('Why do arms get longer after 40?'), not total mysteries or obvious ones.
limitations: Small fMRI samples; trivia questions, not stories or ads.

title: Nostalgia: Past, present, and future
authors: Sedikides, C., Wildschut, T., Arndt, J., Routledge, C.
key_findings: Nostalgia = sentimental longing for one's past; predominantly positive, self-relevant, social emotion.
Narratives feature the self as protagonist among close others, often with a redemption sequence (bad start -> good end).
Triggered by negative mood and especially loneliness; raises positive affect, self-esteem, social connectedness, and buffers existential threat.
Over 80% of British undergraduates reported nostalgia at least weekly.
practical_applications: Nostalgia content (first pair of glasses, grandparent reading with glasses) should centre on people, not objects, and end on warmth.
limitations: Mostly Western student samples in early work; short review.

title: Self-determination theory and the facilitation of intrinsic motivation, social development, and well-being
authors: Ryan, R. M., Deci, E. L.
key_findings: Three innate psychological needs - competence, autonomy, relatedness - when satisfied yield enhanced self-motivation and well-being.
Focus on social contexts that facilitate vs forestall self-motivation.
practical_applications: Characters grow when they choose (autonomy), get better at something (competence) and feel connected (relatedness); ads that pressure undermine autonomy.
limitations: Abstract-level only this session.

title: Basic psychological need satisfaction, need frustration, and need strength across four cultures
authors: Chen, B., Vansteenkiste, M., et al.
key_findings: Study 1: late adolescents in Belgium and China (N = 685, mean age 17); Study 2: Belgium, China, USA, Peru (N = 1,051, mean age 20).
Satisfaction of each need (autonomy, relatedness, competence) uniquely predicted well-being; frustration of each uniquely predicted ill-being.
Effects were equivalent across the four countries and not moderated by need valuation or need desire.
practical_applications: Supports using SDT needs in Thai content too (cross-cultural, incl. an East Asian sample).
limitations: Students/young adults; no Thai sample; cross-sectional.

title: Maslow reconsidered: A review of research on the need hierarchy theory
authors: Wahba, M. A., Bridwell, L. G.
key_findings: Review of ten factor-analytic and three ranking studies gave only partial support for Maslow.
No clear evidence for five distinct need categories or for a fixed hierarchy; some evidence for two types (deficiency vs growth).
practical_applications: Don't present Maslow's pyramid as proven science in content.
limitations: Old review; title taken from common citation, not confirmed on page this session.

title: Needs and subjective well-being around the world
authors: Tay, L., Diener, E.
key_findings: Data from 123 countries: fulfilment of Maslow-type needs correlates with well-being across cultures.
The order in which needs are met has little bearing on their contribution; people report social and self-actualisation needs met even when basic needs are not fully met.
practical_applications: Belonging and respect matter even to customers under money pressure; don't assume 'price first, feelings later'.
limitations: Known only via university press release and coverage this session.

title: Psychology 2e (sections 9.2 Lifespan Theories, 9.3 Stages of Development, 10.1 Motivation, 12.4 Conformity, Compliance, and Obedience)
authors: Spielman, R. M., Jenkins, W. J., Lovett, M. D.
key_findings: Erikson: generativity vs stagnation (30-64) and integrity vs despair (65+); stage theories increasingly replaced by continuous, context-dependent views.

Middle adulthood: visual acuity decreases; crystallized intelligence stable or rising. Late adulthood: fluid intelligence and processing speed decline; networks shrink but remaining friendships stay as close or closer (Carstensen SST).
Motivation: overjustification effect strongest for expected tangible rewards; Yerkes-Dodson; self-efficacy; Maslow criticised for rigid ordering.
Asch: 76% conformed at least once; one dissenter cuts conformity near zero; normative vs informational influence; Milgram 65%, lower when victim closer.
practical_applications: Customers 40+ are in the generativity stage - stories about helping grandchildren/teaching fit.
One honest 'dissenting' voice in a group story is enough to break conformity.
limitations: Intro textbook; page states CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 and forbids use for training generative AI without permission - paraphrase only, do not copy text.
license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 per page footer (search snippet of preface said CC BY 4.0 - conflicting)

title: How replicable are links between personality traits and consequential life outcomes? The Life Outcomes of Personality Replication Project
authors: Soto, C. J.
key_findings: Preregistered replications of 78 Big Five trait-outcome associations (median N = 1,504).
~87% replicated in expected direction; effects ~77% as strong as originals.
practical_applications: Big Five is a sound base for character bibles (e.g. Mint high openness, Tao high conscientiousness).
limitations: Cross-sectional self-report online samples.

title: Cautionary comments regarding the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator
authors: Pittenger, D. J.
key_findings: Insufficient evidence for the tenets of and claims about the MBTI.
Forcing continuous traits into dichotomous types weakens construct validity; earlier work reported 5-week retest type stability of 39-76% depending on dichotomy.
practical_applications: MBTI letters may be used as a playful pop-culture hook only, never as science.
limitations: Publisher (Myers-Briggs Co.) and some commentators dispute the reliability critique.

title: Culture and conformity: A meta-analysis of studies using Asch's (1952b, 1956) line judgment task
authors: Bond, R., Smith, P. B.
key_findings: 68 reports, 133 Asch-type experiments, 4,627 participants, 17 countries (97 of the studies from the USA).
Unweighted mean d = 1.06 (median 0.96); strong heterogeneity (Q = 450.8, df 132).
US conformity has declined since the 1950s; collectivist countries tended to show higher conformity than individualist ones (three individualism-collectivism surveys).
practical_applications: In a collectivist context like Thailand, 'what people like us do' may carry extra weight - but test it.
limitations: Unbalanced sample (79 US studies); no Thai data noted.

title: A room with a viewpoint: Using social norms to motivate environmental conservation in hotels
authors: Goldstein, N. J., Cialdini, R. B., Griskevicius, V.
key_findings: Two hotel field experiments on towel-reuse signs.
Exp. 1: descriptive-norm sign ('almost 75% of guests reuse') 44.1% reuse vs standard environmental sign 35.1% (chi2(1, N = 433) = 3.72, p = .05).

Exp. 2: descriptive norms combined 44.5% vs standard 37.2%; provincial norm ('guests in this room') 49.3% vs the other descriptive norms 42.8% (N = 1,318); citizen (43.5%), gender (40.9%) and guest (44.0%) identity norms did not differ from one another.
practical_applications: Real, local social proof ('many Hua Hin customers choose ...') - only when true.
limitations: German replication succeeded (Bohner & Schlueter 2014); a US resort study found the provincial-norm advantage non-significant.
Read from the University of Minnesota Carlson School copy.

title: The Minimal Group Paradigm and its maximal impact in research on social categorization
authors: Otten, S.
key_findings: Current Opinion in Psychology 11, 85-89 (short review).
The Minimal Group Paradigm studies social categorization with arbitrary, novel groups and no realistic conflict of interest; it shaped Social Identity Theory and Self-Categorization Theory.
Recent variants extend it beyond in-group favouritism/discrimination to many other research fields.
practical_applications: Simple shared labels ('glasses people', 'Hua Hin locals') can create in-group warmth; avoid out-group mocking.
limitations: Title and details known via search summary only.

title: An integrative model of organizational trust
authors: Mayer, R. C., Davis, J. H., Schoorman, F. D.
key_findings: Conceptual model with research propositions (not an empirical test).
Trust = willingness to be vulnerable to another party, distinguished from trustworthiness and from risk-taking.
Perceived trustworthiness = ability, benevolence, integrity; the trustor's propensity to trust also affects trust.
practical_applications: Shop content should show all three: skill (accurate eye test), care (staff go extra), integrity (honest advice, e.g. 'you don't need new lenses yet').
limitations: Later reviewers question whether all three facets have unique effects.

title: Hope theory: Rainbows in the mind
authors: Snyder, C. R.
key_findings: Hope = agency (goal-directed energy) + pathways (planning routes to goals), anchored by goals.
High-hope people generate alternate pathways when blocked; pathways and agency feed each other.
practical_applications: Hopeful stories show a goal, a blocked route, and a new route - not just positive feelings.
limitations: Known via secondary sources; commentaries (Aspinwall & Leaf) question overlap with optimism/self-efficacy.

title: Appealing to fear: A meta-analysis of fear appeal effectiveness and theories
authors: Tannenbaum, M. B., Hepler, J., Zimmerman, R. S., et al.
key_findings: 127 papers (9% unpublished), 248 independent samples, N = 27,372.
Average effect on attitudes/intentions/behaviours d = 0.27 fixed-effects [0.25, 0.30]; random-effects d = 0.29 [0.22, 0.35] (attitudes 0.23, intentions 0.31, behaviours 0.27).

Efficacy statements increased effectiveness (95% CI 0.41-0.49 with vs 0.16-0.22 without), but fear appeals without efficacy did NOT backfire on average: significant negative effects in 9/154 low-efficacy vs 3/94 high-efficacy studies (n.s., Fisher p = .54) - the weak, not the strong, efficacy hypothesis was supported.
High vs moderate depicted fear: d = 0.02 [-0.05, 0.09] (21 samples) - no gain from more fear beyond moderate, and no backfire.
More effective when high susceptibility and severity were depicted, for one-time (vs repeated) behaviours, and for audiences that were more female, from collectivist cultures, or young adults.
practical_applications: Fear (e.g. UV / pterygium risk) can persuade, but pair it with a clear, easy action.
limitations: EPPM-specific results and moderators not read this session.
Read the 2015 UIUC dissertation (IDEALS) on which the Psychological Bulletin article is based - same sample counts; published numbers may differ slightly.

title: Putting the fear back into fear appeals: The extended parallel process model
authors: Witte, K.
key_findings: Communication Monographs 59(4). Theory paper: integrates Janis, Leventhal and Rogers into the Extended Parallel Process Model (EPPM), based on Leventhal's danger control / fear control framework.

Per the abstract it aims to explain why fear appeals fail (boomerang/curvilinear results), re-incorporates fear as a central variable, and states threat-efficacy relations as propositions for future research.
Standard EPPM summary (secondary): high threat + high efficacy -> danger control; high threat + low efficacy -> fear control (denial, avoidance).
practical_applications: Every scare message needs response efficacy and self-efficacy ('a UV400 lens blocks it; come in for a free check').
limitations: Known via encyclopedia and citing meta-analysis (Bigsby & Albarracin 2021) only.
Only the abstract (via OpenAlex) was read. The threat x efficacy predictions are propositions; Tannenbaum2015 found no average backfire for low-efficacy messages.

title: Empathy (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
authors: Stueber, K. (author name not shown in fetched text)
key_findings: Distinguishes emotional contagion, empathy proper (with self-other distinction), cognitive empathy/perspective taking, sympathy/empathic concern, and personal distress.
Batson's empathy-altruism hypothesis: empathic concern produces altruistic motivation ('easy escape' studies); critics propose egoistic alternatives.
Prinz and Bloom: empathy is biased toward the near, similar, cute, in-group and identifiable individual; perspective taking has more positive effects than affective empathy alone.
practical_applications: Show one specific person (identifiable) to evoke empathy, but avoid making the audience feel personal distress (they look away).
limitations: Only the first ~100k of ~150k characters read; author name not confirmed on page (first published 2008, revised 2025).

title: Empathy: A review of the concept
authors: Cuff, B. M. P., Brown, S. J., Taylor, L., Howat, D. J.
key_findings: Review of 43 discrete definitions of empathy; eight themes: distinguishing empathy from other concepts, cognitive or affective, congruent or incongruent, subject to other stimuli, self-other distinction or merging, trait or state, behavioural outcome, automatic or controlled.
Separates empathy from related concepts such as sympathy and proposes a new integrated conceptualisation.
practical_applications: Say which kind of empathy a scene targets: feel-with (affective) or understand (cognitive).
limitations: Full text not accessed (core.ac.uk returned 403).
Read from the Northampton repository author version.

title: The origins of attachment theory: John Bowlby and Mary Ainsworth
authors: Bretherton, I.
key_findings: Bowlby built attachment theory from ethology, control systems, information processing and psychoanalysis; Ainsworth added the secure-base concept and the first empirical study (Uganda).
Internal working models of self and others let people predict the world; out-of-date models after drastic change can cause problems.
Attachment is not regression - it serves a healthy function in adult life too.
practical_applications: Characters' reactions to separation/loss (a parent's old glasses) follow attachment logic: seeking proximity, protest, then reorganisation.
limitations: Historical review, not evidence synthesis.

title: Romantic love conceptualized as an attachment process
authors: Hazan, C., Shaver, P.
key_findings: Applied Ainsworth's three styles to adult romance; adult style distribution roughly matched infancy; styles linked to different love experiences.
practical_applications: Secure / anxious / avoidant as a lens for character dynamics in dialogue stories.
limitations: Early questionnaire studies; later work uses dimensional (anxiety x avoidance) measures (Fraley & Shaver 2000).

title: Cross-cultural patterns of attachment: A meta-analysis of the Strange Situation
authors: van IJzendoorn, M. H., Kroonenberg, P. M.
key_findings: Child Development 59, 147-156: 32 samples from 8 countries, 1,990 Strange Situation classifications, analysed with correspondence analysis.
Intracultural variation was nearly 1.5 times the cross-cultural variation; samples from one country sometimes resembled other countries more than each other.
Avoidant (A) classifications were relatively more prevalent in Western European countries; resistant (C) relatively more frequent in Israel and Japan.
practical_applications: Don't stereotype Thai or 'Asian' families as one attachment type.
limitations: Old, few countries, no Thai sample.

title: Emotional intelligence: New ability or eclectic traits?
authors: Mayer, J. D., Salovey, P., Caruso, D. R.
key_findings: Ability-model authors (Mayer, Salovey, Caruso) agree the term EI is used too all-inclusively and describe much mixed-model ('EQ') research as a 'degenerating research program'.
They cite popular claims as extraordinary: EI 'as powerful, and at times more powerful, than IQ' (Goleman 1995) and 'nearly 90%' of star-performer differences due to EI (Goleman 1998).
They argue a valid, narrower ability concept of EI exists and recommend restricting the term to it.
practical_applications: Use 'EQ' as everyday language for empathy/self-control, not as a measured score that predicts success.
limitations: Proponents with royalty interest in MSCEIT; title from common citation not confirmed on page.

title: Emotional Intelligence: Why It Can Matter More Than IQ
authors: Goleman, D.
key_findings: Existence confirmed (Bantam Books, 1995). Content not read this session.
practical_applications: Popular framing only; the 'matters more than IQ' claim is contested (see Mayer2008_EI).
limitations: Popular science book, mixed-model EI.

title: The Social Animal (12th ed.)
authors: Aronson, E., Aronson, J.
key_findings: Existence and edition confirmed (Worth Publishers). Content not read this session.
practical_applications: Readable social-psychology reference for the team; verify specific studies.
limitations: Not read.

title: The positivity effect: a negativity bias in youth fades with age
authors: Carstensen, L. L., DeLiema, M.
key_findings: Older adults attend to and remember positive information more than negative (positivity effect); authors argue it reflects motivational change, not cognitive/neural decline.

Socioemotional selectivity theory: limited time horizons shift goals toward emotional meaning and satisfaction; age differences in social-partner preferences were eliminated when time horizons were statistically controlled or experimentally expanded.
Considerable evidence that cognitive load reduces the positivity effect; knowing what reduces/enhances it can inform health and education messages for older people.
practical_applications: For 50+ customers, emotionally meaningful, positively framed messages (seeing grandchildren's faces, reading with ease) may land better than threat-heavy ones.
limitations: PMC page blocked by captcha; title from search summary; cross-cultural generality debated (e.g. Japan vs US).

title: Stereotype embodiment: A psychosocial approach to aging
authors: Levy, B. R.
key_findings: Stereotype embodiment theory: age stereotypes (a) are internalized across the life span, (b) can operate unconsciously, (c) gain salience from self-relevance, (d) work through multiple pathways (psychological, behavioural, physiological).
Experimental and longitudinal studies: positive and negative age stereotypes held by older people have beneficial and detrimental effects on cognitive and physical outcomes.
Central message: the ageing process is in part a social construct.
practical_applications: Never show reading glasses as 'getting old and useless'; show capable, active older people.
limitations: Some supporting experiments used subliminal priming - a method hit by the replication crisis; full text not read (PMC captcha).

title: Patient and economic burden of presbyopia: A systematic literature review
authors: Berdahl, J., Bala, C., Dhariwal, M., Lemp-Hull, J., Thakker, D., Jawla, S.
key_findings: 53 studies; uncorrected presbyopia linked to up to 22% lower QoL score and ~80% difficulty with near tasks (Holden 2008).
Psychosocial: distress and low self-esteem reported; in one Chinese study 15% reported low sense of accomplishment and 7% shame/embarrassment.
Correction rates range from 6% (Africa) to 84% (North America); cost and inconvenience are barriers.
practical_applications: Presbyopia content can name quiet embarrassment (holding the phone at arm's length) with warmth, not ridicule.
limitations: Funded by Alcon with employee authors; English-only, mostly cross-sectional; psychological evidence thin.

title: Gorillas in our midst: Sustained inattentional blindness for dynamic events
authors: Simons, D. J., Chabris, C. F.
key_findings: People engaged in a monitoring task often miss an obvious unexpected event; harder tasks produce more misses.
Unexpected events similar to the attended features are noticed more.
practical_applications: In busy frames viewers miss the product; give the glasses the single focus of attention.
limitations: Details via secondary summaries this session.

title: Planting misinformation in the human mind: A 30-year investigation of the malleability of memory
authors: Loftus, E. F.
key_findings: Misleading post-event information impairs memory of the original event (misinformation effect).
Warnings help only under limited circumstances; effects stronger when attention is limited.
Young children and the elderly are more susceptible than younger adults; people can come to believe rich false events.
practical_applications: Memory is reconstructive - flashback scenes can 'change' as characters retell them; never use this to mislead customers.
limitations: Narrative review by the field's leading proponent.

title: Can people feel happy and sad at the same time?
authors: Larsen, J. T., McGraw, A. P., Cacioppo, J. T.
doi_isbn: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
key_findings: Usually people report one or the other, but after Life Is Beautiful, moving out, or graduating many felt both happy and sad.
Affect is typically bipolar in experience but underlying processes are bivariate; later work: making endings salient heightens mixed emotions.
practical_applications: Bittersweet endings ('last day before retirement', 'old frames retired') are a valid, documented emotion state for stories.
limitations: Self-report studies.

title: The spotlight effect in social judgment: An egocentric bias in estimates of the salience of one's own actions and appearance
authors: Gilovich, T., Medvec, V. H., Savitsky, K.
key_findings: People overestimate how many others notice their appearance (embarrassing T-shirt) and actions; anchoring-and-adjustment explanation.
practical_applications: Addresses fear of 'looking old in reading glasses' or bold frames: others notice less than you think - a kind, true reassurance.
limitations: Student samples; details via secondary summaries.

title: Emotion regulation: Current status and future prospects
authors: Gross, J. J.
key_findings: Process model sorts strategies by where they act in emotion generation (situation selection/modification, attentional deployment, cognitive change/reappraisal, response modulation).
Extended model: regulation as valuation with identification, selection, implementation stages.
practical_applications: A character who reappraises ('it's not age, it's just focus') vs one who suppresses gives two clear arcs.
limitations: Abstract-level only; field still debates what 'emotion regulation' covers.

title: The role of transportation in the persuasiveness of public narratives
authors: Green, M. C., Brock, T. C.
key_findings: Introduced 'transportation' - absorption into a story - as a route by which stories change beliefs toward story content.
practical_applications: Stories persuade when immersive; product claims inside a story should be story-true, not a jarring ad break.
limitations: Known via handbook citation only.

title: The extended transportation-imagery model: A meta-analysis of the antecedents and consequences of consumers' narrative transportation
authors: van Laer, T., de Ruyter, K., Visconti, L. M., Wetzels, M.
key_findings: Meta-analysis of 132 effect sizes from 76 published and unpublished articles.
Storyteller antecedents of transportation: identifiable characters r = .20, imaginable plot .29, verisimilitude .27; receiver: transportability .30, attention .29, familiarity .21; age had no effect.
Effects of transportation: affective responses .57 (large), attitudes .44, intentions .31, beliefs .26, narrative thoughts .20, critical thoughts -.20.
Fail-safe N 80-6,627; studies using the Transportation scale showed smaller effects (.34) than other scales (.56).
practical_applications: Supports story-first carousels/clips as a persuasion format.
limitations: Specific effect sizes not read this session.
Read from the City University accepted manuscript; 43% of studies did not report age and 33% had mean age 18-22.

title: A re-examination of the mere exposure effect: The influence of repeated exposure on recognition, familiarity, and liking
authors: Montoya, R. M., Horton, R. S., Vevea, J. L., Citkowicz, M., Lauber, E. A.
key_findings: 268 curves from 81 articles: liking rises with exposure then falls (inverted-U).
Existing models do not adequately account for the findings.
practical_applications: Repeat brand elements (wordmark, Mint & Tao) consistently, but vary execution to avoid wear-out.
limitations: Abstract-level only.

title: The identifiable victim effect: A meta-analytic review
authors: Lee, S., Feeley, T. H.
key_findings: 41 studies: significant but small effect (r = .05); stronger when the victim bears little responsibility and with money requests.
Later reanalysis (Maier et al. 2023, secondary) found moderate evidence of publication bias.
practical_applications: One named person helps, but the effect is small - don't rely on it alone.
limitations: Abstract-level; publication bias concern.
